nodes.statement: We now provide some intuitions behind the design of CorePolyC. item Loop bound. In CorePolyC, we completely prohibit unbounded loop statements, such as while(true)\...\, which run the risk of non-termination. Such a trade-off is acceptable, since the bounded loops together with the size operation mirror widespread programming practices: loops with explicit iteration ranges (e.g., for(auto i: vec)\dots\ and for i in range(n)\dots\) dominate array/matrix algorithms and dynamic programming. They also fit well within some programming practices, where explicit resource parameterization, such as specifying security parameters, is standard. item The size operator. The loop bound must be a size expression. Without this constraint, we would be able to write a loop statement for(i<x)\dots\. The loop body can be executed Theta(2^sizex) times (exponential in the bit-size of x), which defeats the polynomial time computability restriction we set out. item Absence of multiplication. If the multiplication operator * is admitted in CorePolyC, one can design the following code snippet. x=2; for(i<size(z)) x=x*x; It effectively implements the function zmapsto 2^2^sizez, which takes exponential time to output this number. Therefore, the multiplication operator must be prohibited in our language. As a comparison, Example~ provides a valid implementation of multiplication in CorePolyC. A more general discussion of operations will be presented in Section~. item Iterable variables and expressions. If we do not impose these distinctions between the iterable and the non-iterable variables, the following code would be legitimate. for(i<size(z)) y=x; for(i<size(y)) x=x+x; The program calculates the function (x,z) mapsto 2^sizex(2^sizez-1) x whose size grows exponentially. In this work, we employ a specialized type system (iterable types) to avoid this problematic scenario.

nodes.statement: Fig.~ gives two programs in the style of CorePolyC that intend to implement the fast multiplication of two positive integer variables x, y. [t] 0.45linewidth [xleftmargin=1em,xrightmargin=1em] int main(int x,int y) iint o; for(i<size(y)) if(y o=o+x; else x=x+x; y=y/2; return o; hspace10mm 0.45linewidth [xleftmargin=1em,xrightmargin=1em] int main(int x,int y) int o; iint z; z=y; for(i<size(z)) if(y o=o+x; else x=x+x; y=y/2; return o; captionTwo CorePolyC implementations of fast multiplication. The left one violates the rules~trefLoop and~trefAsgmt, while the right one is well-typed. Both programs are well-formed but only the right one is well-typed. The left program violates the rules~trefLoop and~trefAsgmt, because the non-iterable variable y appears as the parameter of size operation, and the iterable variable o is modified in the loop body. Note that the program on the right declares an iterable variable z. Therefore, this part of the code cannot be placed inside a loop to achieve the effect of for(i<size(z)) x=x*x;, which, as we have explained earlier, should be prohibited. This is also equivalent to defining a function mul(x, y) and attempting to invoke it within a loop. In Section~, we will discuss how to introduce function calls in PolyC to prevent such constructions.

nodes.statement: We start by recalling the definition of Turing machines. A Turing machine M is a 6-tuple (Q, \0,1\, Lambda, delta, q_0, q_halt), where item Q is a finite set of states, item Lambda=\0,1, square\ where square is the blank symbol, item q_0,q_haltin Q are the start state and the halt state, respectively. item delta:QtimesLambdato QtimesLambdatimes\L,R\ is the transition function of M. The Turing machine M has a single, one-way infinite tape and behaves in a standard manner. Its configuration is represented by uqw, where q is the current state, uwinLambda^* is the current tape content, and the head points at the first symbol of w. When M halts, the head will return to the leftmost position, and the content on the tape represents the computation result. Given M=(Q, \0,1\, Lambda, delta, q_0, q_halt) whose running time is given by a polynomial T(n). There is a constant d such that T(n)le dn^d. We construct a program p with input variable x as follows: paragraphConfiguration. We use an mathttint variable y and the input variable x to present the contents of the tape in ternary representation, where the symbols 0, 1, and square are represented by the digits 0, 1, and 2, respectively. The value of y represents the contents to the left of the head, while the value of x represents the contents to the right of the head. For convenience, the digits of x are in reverse order so that the least significant digit of x represents the content under the tape head. Since the most significant digit cannot be 0, we add an extra 2 at the beginning of x and y. Additionally, we declare an mathttint variable q to simulate the state of M. W.l.o.g., we assume that Q=\q_0,q_1,q_2,cdots,q_sizeQ-1\, where q_1=q_halt. paragraphInput and Initialization. Assume that the input on the tape are win\0,1\^*. Let w'=2circ w^r, where w^r represents the reverse of w. Interpret w' as a ternary number and convert it to the corresponding decimal number v, which will serve as the input to p. We declare an int variable y and assign it the value 2. For example, if the input of M is w=10010, then w'=(201001)_3 and v=(514)_10. paragraphTimer. We utilize the method presented in the proof of Lemma to generate a value whose length grows to dsizev^d, and assign it to an iterable variable cnt. Then we design a statement of the form for(i<size(cnt))\ dots \ such that every Turing machine operation is simulated in an iteration of the loop. paragraphSimulation. Inside the loop body, we simulate delta by a sequence of conditional statements. M will only modify its state once in each step. Therefore, we declare a boolean variable flag at the beginning of the loop body to indicate whether q has been updated. For a given constant m, we introduce the syntax sugar m*a, which means a+dots+a (m occurrences of a). item Read. For any transition delta(q_i, alpha), where ine1, we use the following conditions to simulate the tape’s reading and state recognition. If they match, the statement inside \\ simulates the instructions to be executed. if(!flag \&\& q==i \&\& x\%3==alpha) \dots\. item Write. If M needs to change the content to betainLambda and update the state to q_j, it can be done by executing x=x-alpha+beta'; q=j; flag=true;, where beta' is corresponding to beta, i.e., if betain\0,1\, then beta'=beta; otherwise beta'=2. Set flag to \#mathttt to skip the remaining conditional statements. item Leftward Movement. If the head of M needs to move left, the last digit of y is appended to the end of x. However, it is important to note that if the tape head is already at the leftmost position, no movement is performed. This process can be simulated as follows: if(y>2) \x=3*x+y\%3; y=y/3;\ else \\ In base three, the value of y always begins with 2, representing the leftmost end of the tape (square). item Rightward Movement. The rightward movement is simulated by appending the last digit of x to the end of y. If the head is in the rightmost position, it can still move right. In this case, the head will point to a blank symbol square, so we should append digit 2 to the end of y. y=3*y+x\%3; x=x/3; if(x<=2) \x=3*x+2\ else \\ item Halt and Output. We do not add any statements for q_1. Once the program enters this state, it performs no operations until the loop terminates. Add return x; at the end of p to return the encoded output. For example, assuming delta(q_0,0)=(q_1,1,mathttL) and delta(q_0,1)=(q_3,0,mathttR), the corresponding simulation statements are shown in Figure . Since delta is defined on QtimesLambda, the number of conditional statements is at most 3sizeQ. Hence, the entire simulation process can be constructed in polynomial time. [t] 0.48linewidth [xleftmargin=1em,xrightmargin=1em] for(i<size(cnt)) bool flag; // ... if(!flag&&q==0&&x x=x-0+1; q=1; flag=true; if(y>2) x=3*x+y y=y/3; else else // other transitions... hspace10mm 0.48linewidth [xleftmargin=1em,xrightmargin=1em] for(i<size(cnt)) bool flag; // ... if(!flag&&q==0&&x x=x-1+0; q=3; flag=true; if(x>2) y=3*y+x x=x/3; else y=3*y+2; else // other transitions... captionExamples of the simulation process. The left program simulates the transition delta(q_0,0)=(q_1,1,mathttL), , while the right one simulates the transition delta(q_0,1)=(q_3,0,mathttR). The program p fully simulates the computation of M. Since the tape head of M eventually returns to the leftmost position, the reversed ternary representation of the output without the last digit corresponds to the output of M.

nodes.statement: In the Knapsack problem, given m items with positive integer weights w_1, ldots, w_m and positive integer values c_1, ldots, c_m, it is asked to find a subset of items such that the sum of their weights does not exceed a given positive integer W, and the total value is maximized. nodes.name: Graph Reachability Problem
nodes.statement: The PATH problem asks whether there exists a path from a given source node s to a target node t in a directed graph G=(V,E). The problem can be solved by an O(sizeV+sizeE)-time Depth-First Search algorithm (DFS). nodes.name: Sorting Problem
nodes.statement: The input for sorting algorithms is an array A, and the goal is to rearrange the elements' positions so that they are sorted in non-decreasing or non-increasing order. There are various sorting algorithms, and typically, their average time complexity is Theta(nlog n), where n is the number of elements in the array. The proofs for the other cases follow a similar pattern to those of Lemma \ref{lem:expr-size}.

Secondly, we further demonstrate that the corresponding conclusions hold for statements with $D=i+1$.
